cards.explanation: The answer is the wilderness. The song asks, "Who is this coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved?" She's coming up out of the wilderness, and she's leaning on her beloved. I think that says something good about whoever she's leaning on, friends. My mustache has carried a lot of cookie boxes, but it has never once held up a person.

The answer is that love is as strong as death. Right after the request to be set as a seal, the song gives its reason: "For love is as strong as death…" That's a big comparison, because death is about the strongest thing a person can name. The seal request and the strength of love are tied together in the same breath. That's a lot of weight for one little stamp to carry, and I would know.

The answer is False. The song calls love's sparks "…fiery flames, the fiercest blaze of all." That's the biggest fire it can name, and nothing in the verse says it fades. A flame like that doesn't sound like it's running out of steam to me, friends. And the very next verse says water can't put it out.

The answer is that mighty waters cannot quench it. The song says it flat out: "Mighty waters cannot quench love…" You'd think a flood could handle any fire. Not this one. Water is supposed to win that fight, friends, and here it just doesn't.

The answer is True. The song says that if a man were to give "…all the wealth of his house for love, his offer would be utterly scorned." That's a big pile of wealth, and it still buys nothing. Love isn't something money can purchase. Even a whole house full of treasure can't pay for it.

The answer is what to do for her when she is spoken for. The speakers ask, "What shall we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for?" They're planning ahead for that day. Somebody in the family is already thinking about the big day. That's the kind of family huddle I know very well.

The answer is like one who brings peace. She says, "So I have become in his eyes like one who brings peace." She talks about being a wall, then says she has become like one who brings peace in his eyes. I think that's a nice place to land, friends.

The answer is True. The speaker says, "But my own vineyard is mine to give; the thousand shekels are for you, O Solomon…" So the thousand shekels are for Solomon, the one being spoken to. The same speaker says the vineyard is theirs to give. That's someone who knows exactly where those shekels are headed, and I respect that.

The answer is those who tend its fruit. The speaker says, "…two hundred are for those who tend its fruit." A thousand is for Solomon, and two hundred is for those who tend its fruit. Both amounts get named in the same verse.

The answer is False. The speaker says, "You who dwell in the gardens, my companions are listening for your voice. Let me hear it!" So the speaker asks for the voice, not for silence. Everybody's waiting to hear it. If anyone's whispering "shh" in this verse, it isn't the speaker.

The answer is a gazelle or a young stag. The last line says, "Come away, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices." Both are quick on their feet. The song asks the beloved to be like them, and it ends on that picture of the mountains of spices. It's a good last line for a whole song, friends.
